_about: Ceilings and floors for advisory warnings. Each rule states what the number means and what crossing it signals - not the project it was seeded from, which is recorded in the commit that introduced it and in git history. Seeded values are starting points, not laws: run the tool for a few weeks, read the direction of travel, then set the limits where your project actually sits. Every edit here is a diff, which is the point. Delete any rule to silence it.

commentRatio.why: Comment share of product source. SonarQube retired its 25% comment-density rule because a floor there encouraged filler; a ceiling at the same level is where generated prose starts to outrun the code it describes. The ratchet against your own baseline is the real instrument; this ceiling only says when to stop and look.

docProseToCode.why: Documentation prose per line of product code. At 1.0 the repository carries a prose line for every code line, so prose must be updated at least as often as behaviour - the condition under which documentation becomes the thing that makes a small change expensive.

agentContextLines.why: Repo-local instruction text: AGENTS.md, repo-local skills, repo-local agent definitions. Every line enters context on every session, so this is a tax paid before any work starts. Global skills and the user's harness agents are reported separately and never ratcheted, because a repository cannot gate what it does not own.

assertsPerTestCase.why: Assertions per test case. A floor above zero catches tests that execute code without checking anything. Kept deliberately low: assertion density is a style choice rather than a health signal, so any higher floor encodes a preference and produces false alarms on healthy suites.

linesPerTestCase.why: Test lines per test case. A very high figure suggests fixtures or setup dominating rather than assertions. Deliberately loose and ambiguous in sign - heavy tests are sometimes the correct choice - so treat a warning here as a prompt to look, not a defect.

testRatio.why: Test lines per line of product code. Above parity the suite costs more to keep compiling than the behaviour it protects, and every structural change pays for all of it. Watch the direction of travel: a ratio climbing while code shrinks means tests are being added to tests.
